mcqs.question: What's the actual test for whether an abstraction's boundary is drawn in the right place?
options: Whether the implementation is written in fewer than 50 lines of code
Whether the method has a short, memorable name
Whether the implementation could change completely without any caller needing to notice or change
Whether the method is declared in an interface rather than a concrete class
mcqs.explanation: A good abstraction lets the implementation swap freely (quicksort for timsort, one payment provider for another) without callers caring, because the contract — not the mechanism — is what they depend on. Line count, naming, and whether it happens to be declared in an interface don't determine whether the hiding is actually effective.

mcqs.question: What's the key difference between an interface and an abstract class as abstraction mechanisms?
options: An interface is pure contract with no implementation, while an abstract class can mix a contract with some shared, already-written behavior
An abstract class cannot declare any methods, only fields
An interface can only be implemented by exactly one class
Interfaces are only usable for abstraction, while abstract classes cannot express abstraction at all
mcqs.explanation: An interface commits to zero implementation — just method signatures — while an abstract class can provide real, shared method bodies alongside methods subclasses must still fill in. Abstract classes absolutely can declare methods, interfaces can be implemented by many classes, and both are legitimate abstraction tools.

mcqs.question: A teammate asks: "Is hiding a payment provider behind a `PaymentProcessor` interface abstraction or encapsulation?" What's the accurate answer?
options: Encapsulation, because interfaces are always about protecting internal state
Neither — interfaces don't relate to either concept
Both terms mean the same thing here, so it doesn't matter which you use
Abstraction — it's about hiding what varies between providers behind a shared contract; encapsulation would be about protecting a class's own internal fields from outside mutation
mcqs.explanation: Hiding which concrete implementation sits behind a contract, so callers don't need to know or care, is abstraction's job. Encapsulation is a separate concern about guarding an object's own state from invalid external mutation — the two often coexist but answer different questions.

mcqs.question: A codebase has an interface with exactly one implementation, added 'because it's best practice,' with no plan for a second implementation. What's the issue?
options: There's no issue — every class should always have an interface regardless of implementation count
It adds a layer of indirection that buys nothing, since there's no variation for the interface to actually hide
Interfaces with one implementation cause runtime performance problems
It means the class violates encapsulation
mcqs.explanation: An interface earns its cost by hiding variation between implementations; with only one implementation and no concrete plan for a second, it's pure indirection with no payoff — extract it later when a real second implementation shows up. It causes no runtime performance issue and has nothing to do with encapsulation.

mcqs.question: An ORM's `.save()` call silently issues 500 individual INSERT statements in a loop, making a page slow. Why is this described as a 'leaky abstraction' rather than just a bug?
options: Because the ORM's source code is publicly visible
Because the caller can no longer call `.save()` at all until the bug is fixed
Because the hidden implementation detail (how many SQL statements run) affects observable behavior the abstraction was supposed to make irrelevant
Because ORMs should never be used in production systems
mcqs.explanation: The abstraction hid the mechanism (SQL generation) but not the consequence (slow page load), so the caller ends up needing to understand SQL and query patterns anyway — exactly what the abstraction promised to avoid. Source visibility, whether the call still works, and blanket anti-ORM claims aren't what defines a leaky abstraction.
